title: People v. Smith (1975)
summary: Under ejusdem generis, "other dangerous weapon" following "dagger, dirk, stiletto" in Michigan's concealed-weapons statute covers only stabbing weapons, so carrying an M-1 rifle in a van is not a crime under that section.
notes: Supreme Court of Michigan, 1975. Key line: "The question is whether this statute proscribes the carrying of all dangerous weapons or only those of the types specified." (Chief Justice T.G. Kavanagh)

sections.Parties: The People of the State of Michigan prosecuted the defendant, Smith, along with three others, including co-defendants Gaut and Turner, for carrying a concealed weapon in a motor vehicle under M.C.L.A. section 750.227. Smith was a passenger in the van where the rifle was found. He moved to quash the charge on the ground that an M-1 rifle, which is more than 30 inches long, is not a "dangerous weapon" within the meaning of the concealed-weapons statute. The prosecution took the position that an M-1 is plainly dangerous and therefore covered.
sections.Material Facts: Detroit Police Officer Ward and his partner watched a Ford Econoline van make several erratic U-turns and stopped it. As Ward approached, he saw through the right window what looked like the stock of a rifle. He opened the door and pulled an M-1 rifle from under the second seat. Smith was sitting on the third seat with his feet up. A cartridge belt and clips of ammunition lay on the front seat between Gaut and Turner. Section 750.227 makes it a felony, punishable by up to five years or a $2,500 fine, to carry "a dagger, dirk, stiletto, or other dangerous weapon except hunting knives adapted and carried as such," concealed on the person or concealed or otherwise in a vehicle, or to carry an unlicensed pistol. A separate statute defines a pistol as a firearm 30 inches or less in length.
sections.Procedural History: After a preliminary examination at which Officer Ward testified, the defendants moved to quash. The trial court denied the motion, reasoning that because the M-1 is a military rifle it falls within the classification of dangerous weapons. The Michigan Court of Appeals majority affirmed without analyzing the statute, saying it had no doubt that when the legislature said "dangerous weapon" it meant dangerous weapon. The Supreme Court of Michigan, in an opinion by Chief Justice T.G. Kavanagh, held that the prosecution erred in charging Smith under section 750.227, because that section does not reach long-barreled firearms.
sections.Issue: Whether a rifle more than 30 inches long, here an M-1, is a "dangerous weapon" within M.C.L.A. section 750.227, which prohibits carrying "a dagger, dirk, stiletto, or other dangerous weapon" concealed on the person or in a vehicle, when the statute is read consistently with the Michigan Constitution and the intent of the legislature.
sections.Holding: No. Under ejusdem generis, the general words "or other dangerous weapon" following the specific stabbing weapons "dagger, dirk, stiletto" are limited to weapons of the same kind, so the phrase does not include firearms of any sort. The M-1 is also not a "pistol," which the code defines as a firearm 30 inches or less in length. Section 750.227 therefore applies only to the weapons it enumerates, and long rifles are instead governed by section 750.226, which punishes going armed with any firearm with intent to use it unlawfully.
sections.Reasoning: The Chief Justice reframed the question. No one disputed that an M-1 is dangerous; the issue was whether the statute reaches all dangerous weapons or only the listed types. The court applied ejusdem generis: where general words follow a designation of particular subjects, the general words are presumed restricted to things of the same kind, class, character or nature as those enumerated. "Other dangerous weapon," following dagger, dirk and stiletto and carving out hunting knives, is limited to stabbing weapons. The pistol clause did not help because the code defines a pistol as a firearm 30 inches or less, or one built to conceal that it is a firearm. The court confirmed its reading from the structure of the act: section 750.226 expressly punishes going armed with "a pistol or other firearm" with intent to use it unlawfully, so the legislature had already addressed long guns and placed them in an intent-based offense rather than a concealment offense. Reading section 750.227 to cover rifles would expose weekend hunters to felony prosecution with no unlawful intent. The court was not legalizing carrying M-1 rifles with unlawful intent; the prosecution simply charged under the wrong section. No separate opinion appears.

topics.lrs-k-ejusdem: The court states the canon in full and applies it to confine "other dangerous weapon" to stabbing weapons like the daggers, dirks and stilettos that precede it.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: Section 750.226, which expressly covers "a pistol or other firearm" carried with unlawful intent, shows the legislature had already placed long guns in a different offense, confirming the narrow reading of section 750.227.
topics.lrs-k-absurdity: The court tests the broad reading against its consequences: treating rifles as concealed weapons would make felons of weekend hunters who have no unlawful intent.
topics.lrs-k-lenity: The decision narrows a criminal statute to its enumerated weapons and leaves any broader regulation of long guns to the legislature, though the court does not invoke lenity by name.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The case shows a canon doing real work against a plain-meaning argument that "dangerous weapon" simply means any dangerous weapon.

learning.separateOpinions: None appears; Chief Justice T.G. Kavanagh wrote for the court.
learning.why: The case is the standard illustration of ejusdem generis: a general term at the end of a specific list ("dagger, dirk, stiletto, or other dangerous weapon") is confined to the class of the listed items, and the court confirms the result by reading the neighboring section that expressly covers firearms.
